title: Authentication / Authorization
subtitle: Distinguishing AuthN from AuthZ, stateless JWTs vs stateful sessions, OAuth 2.0 / OIDC, and RBAC vs ABAC vs ReBAC.
keyTakeaways: Authentication (AuthN) verifies who the user is; Authorization (AuthZ) verifies what resources and actions the user is permitted to access.
Stateless JWTs eliminate database lookups at the cost of difficult revocation; stateful sessions in Redis allow instant revocation but require a network hop on every request.
Access control models evolve from simple Role-Based (RBAC) to Attribute-Based (ABAC) and finally Relationship-Based (ReBAC, Google Zanzibar) for collaborative graph permissions.

sections.heading: Stateless JWTs vs Stateful Sessions and Revocation
sections.body: Session management fundamentally trades off verification latency against revocation control. Traditional web applications store a session ID in a cookie and keep the user's session state in a centralized Redis cluster. Modern microservice architectures often favor JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), which are cryptographically signed payloads verified locally by any service using an asymmetric public key.
bullets: Stateful Sessions: When a user changes their password or an administrator bans an account, deleting the session key in Redis instantly logs out the user worldwide. Downside: every single API request must perform a Redis lookup.

Stateless JWTs: Services verify the cryptographic signature locally without querying a central database, making them fast and horizontally scalable. Downside: once issued, a JWT is valid until its expiration timestamp (`exp`). Revoking a compromised token before expiration requires maintaining a revocation blocklist in memory.

The Production Hybrid: Use short-lived JWT access tokens (10-15 minute expiry) paired with long-lived stateful refresh tokens (7-30 days) stored in the database. When the access token expires, the client exchanges the refresh token, allowing the server to enforce bans or permission changes.

sections.heading: Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC, and ReBAC
sections.body: Once identity is proven, the authorization engine determines whether the actor can perform the requested operation on the target resource. As applications grow in complexity, permission models evolve through three distinct architectures.
bullets: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Users are assigned roles (`Admin`, `Editor`, `Viewer`), and roles have static permissions. Simple to manage, but breaks down when permissions depend on context ('Can an Editor edit a document owned by another department?').

Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC): Evaluates dynamic attributes of the user, the resource, and the environment (e.g., 'Allow access if User.Department == Resource.Department AND Request.Time < 18:00'). Highly flexible, but complex to audit and evaluate efficiently.

Relationship-Based Access Control (ReBAC): Pioneered by Google's Zanzibar paper. Permissions are modeled as a graph of relationships (e.g., 'User A is a member of Team B, which owns Folder C, which contains Document D'). Evaluated using high-speed distributed graph traversals.

tradeOffs.pros: Zero database lookups on request paths; microservices verify tokens independently using public keys; scales seamlessly.
tradeOffs.cons: Cannot revoke tokens immediately without maintaining a distributed blocklist; larger payload size over the wire.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-throughput microservice ecosystems, mobile application APIs, and federated Single Sign-On (SSO).

tradeOffs.pros: Instant token revocation across all devices; session metadata can be updated in real time; compact cookie tokens.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires a network round trip to Redis on every single request; session store is a critical dependency for uptime.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Monolithic web apps, administrative banking portals, and sensitive internal enterprise applications.

interviewTip: When discussing authentication in microservices, suggest the short-lived JWT + refresh token pattern: 'We issue short-lived 10-minute JWT access tokens verified locally by microservices without database queries, paired with long-lived refresh tokens checked against a database only once every 10 minutes to verify revocation status.'
